slides.title: Requirements Engineering Fundamentals

blocks.content: Lecture 8: Requirements Engineering Fundamentals
Systematic Approaches to Defining Software Requirements

slides.speakerNotes: Welcome to Lecture 8 on Requirements Engineering. This lecture covers the foundation of successful software projects - understanding and documenting what the system should do. Emphasize that 60-70% of software failures trace back to requirements issues, making this one of the most critical topics in software engineering.

slides.title: What is Requirements Engineering?

blocks.content:
**Requirements Engineering**: Systematic process of defining, documenting, and maintaining software requirements

**Key Impact**: 60-70% of software failures trace to requirements issues

**Core Challenge**: Bridge between stakeholder needs and system implementation

content.title: Analyze: Problem vs. Solution Statements
content.instruction: Classify each statement as a valid requirement (problem-focused) or premature solution. Justify your reasoning.
items: A. The system must process 10,000 transactions per second
B. The system must use Apache Kafka for messaging
C. Users must receive order confirmation within 2 seconds
D. The application must be built with React framework
E. The system must support users in 15 languages
content.explanation: Valid requirements: A (performance NFR), C (performance NFR), E (functional). B and D are implementation solutions, not requirements—they constrain how to build, not what to build. Requirements specify the problem; design specifies the solution.

slides.speakerNotes: After presenting the definition, engage students in analytical thinking about what constitutes a proper requirement. Walk through the activity, emphasizing that requirements describe the problem space (what/why) while design addresses solution space (how). Discuss how B and D might be valid if they're genuine constraints from stakeholders, but typically they're premature design decisions. Connect to real failures: Denver Airport baggage system failed partly because requirements mixed business needs with technical solutions. This distinction is foundational for all subsequent RE activities.

slides.title: The Requirements Engineering Process

content.prompt: Circular process diagram showing four connected activities: Elicitation → Analysis → Specification → Validation, with Requirements Management in the center. Include feedback arrows connecting all activities in both directions. Use professional colors and clear labels.

content.title: Apply: Trace Through the RE Process
content.instruction: A stakeholder requests: 'Users complain checkout takes too long.' Trace this through the RE process—what happens at each stage?
items: Elicitation: What questions would you ask? What techniques?
Analysis: What underlying needs might this reveal?
Specification: Draft one concrete requirement
Validation: How would you verify it's correct?
Management: What if scope changes mid-development?
content.explanation: Sample responses: Elicitation—interview users, observe checkout sessions, ask 'How long is acceptable?' Analysis—need for performance improvement, possibly usability issues. Specification—'Checkout process shall complete in ≤30 seconds for 95% of transactions.' Validation—prototype testing, stakeholder review. Management—trace impact to UI design, backend APIs, test cases.

slides.speakerNotes: Present the process model, then engage students in applying it to a realistic scenario. Walk through each stage, emphasizing the iterative nature—validation might reveal the real problem is confusing UI, not speed, requiring new elicitation. Highlight how one vague complaint transforms through systematic RE into testable requirements. Discuss how different elicitation techniques (observation vs interviews) might yield different insights. Connect to next slide's deep dive into elicitation techniques, noting students will soon learn which techniques work best for different situations.

slides.title: Requirements Elicitation Techniques

items: Interviews: Structured and unstructured conversations
Workshops: Facilitated group sessions for collaboration
Observation: Watching users in natural work environment
Prototyping: Using mockups to elicit feedback
Document Analysis: Reviewing existing systems and regulations

content.title: Apply: Select Elicitation Techniques
content.instruction: For each scenario, choose 2-3 techniques and justify your selection:
items: Medical device software—users are surgeons, strict regulations exist
Consumer mobile app—target users are teenagers, no legacy system
Internal HR system replacement—existing workflows documented, users resistant to change
content.explanation: Sample: Medical device—Document analysis (regulations), observation (OR procedures), structured interviews (safety protocols). Mobile app—Prototyping (visual feedback), workshops (collaborative design), unstructured interviews (exploratory needs). HR system—Document analysis (current workflows), observation (actual vs documented processes), workshops (address resistance). Justifications should reference stakeholder characteristics, domain constraints, and technique strengths.

slides.speakerNotes: Present the five core techniques briefly, then immediately engage students in applying them to realistic contexts. The activity requires analytical thinking—students must consider stakeholder characteristics, domain constraints, and technique strengths/limitations. Emphasize that technique selection is not arbitrary; it depends on project context. Discuss how medical device needs documentation for compliance while teenagers respond better to visual prototypes. This bridges to the next slide's deep dive into interviews and workshops, where students will see how to execute these techniques effectively.

slides.title: Interviews and Workshops

items: Structured: Predefined questions, consistent format
Unstructured: Exploratory, open-ended discussions
Workshops: Facilitated group sessions (JAD, brainstorming)
Open-ended questions uncover unstated needs

content.title: Apply: Design Interview Questions
content.instruction: For this scenario, write 3 interview questions (1 structured, 2 open-ended): You're building a library management system. Your stakeholder is a head librarian who manages circulation, cataloging, and patron services.
items: What makes a good vs. poor question?
How do open-ended questions reveal hidden requirements?
content.explanation: Good structured: 'How many books does your library circulate daily?' (quantifiable). Good open-ended: 'Walk me through what happens when a patron reports a lost book' (reveals workflow); 'What frustrates you most about the current system?' (uncovers pain points). Poor: leading questions, yes/no questions, jargon-heavy phrasing. Open-ended questions let stakeholders describe context, workarounds, and priorities in their own terms.

slides.speakerNotes: After presenting techniques, have students apply them by crafting actual interview questions for a realistic scenario. This moves from understanding what interviews are to applying question design principles. Discuss student responses: structured questions gather facts (circulation volume, staff count), while open-ended questions reveal processes and pain points. Emphasize avoiding leading questions ('Don't you think automated renewals would help?') and closed yes/no questions. For workshops, briefly mention JAD sessions and facilitation techniques like dot voting for prioritization. This prepares students for the observation and prototyping techniques on the next slide.

slides.title: Observation and Prototyping

items: Observation: Watch users in natural environment to uncover tacit knowledge
Contextual inquiry: observation + concurrent interviews
Prototyping: Paper → Wireframes → Interactive mockups
Throwaway vs. evolutionary prototypes

content.title: Apply: Choose Your Technique
content.instruction:
For each scenario, select observation OR prototyping and justify your choice:

A) Hospital emergency room triage system—nurses handle critical decisions under time pressure

B) Consumer mobile app for meal planning—target users are busy parents, feature set uncertain
items: What factors make one technique more suitable?
Could you combine both? How?
content.explanation: A) Observation preferred—triage involves tacit expertise, high-stakes workflows, and context-dependent decisions that nurses may not articulate in interviews. Watching actual triage reveals workarounds and decision patterns. B) Prototyping preferred—uncertain requirements benefit from early feedback; low-fidelity mockups quickly validate feature priorities with parents. Combining both: observe current meal-planning behavior, then prototype solutions based on observed pain points.

slides.speakerNotes: This activity elevates the slide from understand to apply by requiring technique selection and justification for realistic contexts. Guide students to consider: observation excels when processes are tacit, complex, or context-dependent (medical workflows, expert tasks); prototyping works when requirements are uncertain or users struggle to articulate needs abstractly. Discuss how observation reveals what people actually do versus what they say, while prototypes make abstract requirements concrete. Emphasize that techniques often combine—observe first to understand context, then prototype solutions. This bridges to functional requirements on the next slide, where documented behaviors come from elicitation.

slides.title: Functional Requirements

blocks.content:
What the system must do - specific behaviors and functions

• Describe system inputs, outputs, and transformations
• Expressed as 'The system shall...' statements
• Directly testable through functional testing

content.title: Apply: Write Functional Requirements
content.instruction:
A university needs a course registration system. Given these stakeholder needs, write 3 functional requirements using proper format:

• Students want to see which courses fit their schedule
• Professors need to know enrollment numbers
• System must prevent double-booking classrooms
items: Use 'The system shall...' format
Make each requirement atomic and testable
Identify inputs, outputs, or transformations
content.explanation: Sample answers: FR-001: The system shall display a visual schedule showing time conflicts when a student selects a course. FR-002: The system shall provide real-time enrollment counts to instructors for their assigned courses. FR-003: The system shall reject room assignments that create scheduling conflicts for the same location and time slot. Each requirement specifies observable system behavior that can be verified through testing.

slides.speakerNotes: This activity elevates the slide from understand to apply by requiring students to transform stakeholder needs into properly formatted functional requirements. After individual work, share sample answers and discuss common mistakes: vague verbs, multiple requirements in one statement, or non-testable phrasing. Emphasize that good FRs specify observable behavior without prescribing implementation. Ask students to identify the input/output/transformation in each requirement. This directly supports the objective to document requirements using industry standards and bridges to NFRs on the next slide, where quality attributes complement functional behavior.

slides.title: Non-Functional Requirements

blocks.content:
How well the system performs - quality attributes that constrain solutions

• Performance, Security, Usability, Reliability, Maintainability
• Drive architectural decisions (NFRs often determine system structure)
• Must be quantified with measurable criteria
• Categories from ISO 25010 quality model

content.title: Analyze: Categorize & Evaluate Requirements
content.instruction: Examine these requirements. For each: (1) Classify as Functional, Non-Functional, or Constraint, (2) Identify quality issues, (3) Rewrite poorly specified NFRs with measurable criteria.
items: REQ-A: System must be very fast and responsive
REQ-B: System shall generate monthly reports in PDF format
REQ-C: Application must be developed using React framework
REQ-D: System should be easy to use for all users
content.explanation: REQ-A: NFR (performance) - too vague. Better: 'System shall load pages within 1.5 seconds for 95% of requests.' REQ-B: Functional - specifies system behavior. REQ-C: Constraint - mandates technology choice. REQ-D: NFR (usability) - unmeasurable. Better: 'Users shall complete core tasks with ≤3 clicks and no training.' This exercise develops analyze-level skills for distinguishing requirement types and evaluate-level skills for assessing quality against measurability criteria.

slides.speakerNotes: This activity addresses two objectives: distinguishing functional/non-functional requirements (analyze level) and validating requirement quality (evaluate level). After individual work, discuss classifications and common NFR mistakes: vague terms without metrics. Emphasize that NFRs like 'fast' or 'user-friendly' are untestable. Show how quantified NFRs drive architecture: 99.9% availability requires redundancy; sub-second response times may necessitate caching layers. Connect to validation criteria on slide 15 and architectural impact discussions.

slides.title: Constraints and Domain Requirements

blocks.content:
Constraints: Non-negotiable limitations (technology mandates, regulations, budget)
Domain Requirements: Application-specific needs from the problem domain (medical, financial, legal)

Both limit solution space and drive architectural decisions

content.title: Analyze: Classify Requirements
content.instruction: Categorize each requirement as Functional, Non-Functional, Constraint, or Domain Requirement. Justify your classification and identify any that span multiple categories.
items: System must use PostgreSQL 12 or higher
Healthcare records must be retained for 7 years
Users shall reset passwords via email verification
Payment processing must comply with PCI-DSS Level 1
System shall process 10,000 transactions per second
Application must be deployed on AWS infrastructure
content.explanation: PostgreSQL requirement: Constraint (technology mandate). 7-year retention: Domain requirement AND constraint (legal/healthcare domain). Password reset: Functional (system behavior). PCI-DSS: Domain requirement AND constraint (payment domain + regulation). 10K TPS: Non-functional (performance). AWS deployment: Constraint (platform mandate). Some requirements span categories—recognizing overlaps requires analytical thinking about requirement nature and origin.

slides.speakerNotes: This activity addresses the analyze-level objective for distinguishing requirement types. After individual classification, discuss borderline cases that span categories—many domain requirements also function as constraints. Emphasize that constraints narrow design choices (PostgreSQL eliminates NoSQL options), while domain requirements reflect specialized knowledge (HIPAA, PCI-DSS require domain expertise to identify). Connect to slide 8's NFR discussion and slide 10's documentation structure. Ask: How would you discover domain requirements during elicitation? What happens if domain constraints are missed early?

slides.title: Requirements Specification Documents

blocks.content: IEEE 830 / ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 Standard Structure

items: Introduction: Purpose, scope, definitions, overview
Overall Description: Product perspective, functions, user characteristics
Specific Requirements: Detailed functional and non-functional requirements
Appendices: Models, analysis, supporting information

blocks.content: Quality Characteristics: Clear, Unambiguous, Testable, Consistent, Complete

slides.speakerNotes: Introduce the IEEE 830 standard as the industry-standard SRS structure. Emphasize that good requirements documentation follows consistent formats for different audiences. The five quality characteristics are critical: Clear (understandable), Unambiguous (one interpretation), Testable (verifiable), Consistent (no contradictions), Complete (nothing missing). Preview that we'll practice writing quality requirements next.

slides.title: Writing Quality Requirements

items: Modal verbs: 'shall' (mandatory), 'should' (desirable), 'may' (optional)
Avoid ambiguous terms without quantification
One requirement per statement (atomic)
Each requirement must be verifiable

content.code:
❌ Poor: 'The system should be secure and easy to use'

✓ Good: 'The system shall require authentication using 
   username and password before accessing user data'

❌ Poor: 'The system will handle lots of users'

✓ Good: 'The system shall support 10,000 concurrent 
   users with response time < 3 seconds'

slides.speakerNotes: This is a critical skill - writing testable, unambiguous requirements. Walk through the poor vs. good examples. Poor examples use vague terms (secure, easy, lots) and combine multiple requirements. Good examples are specific, quantified, and atomic. Practice exercise: Have students identify problems in poorly-written requirements. Emphasize testability - if you can't verify it, it's not a good requirement.

slides.title: Use Case Fundamentals

blocks.content: Description of system behavior from user perspective to achieve a goal

items: Actors: Users or external systems
Use Cases: Goals the actors want to achieve
Relationships: Include, extend, generalization

content.prompt: UML use case diagram for online shopping system. Show Customer actor (stick figure) connected to use cases: Browse Products, Add to Cart, Checkout, Track Order. Show Admin actor connected to Manage Inventory. Include 'Authenticate User' use case with <<include>> relationship to Checkout. Use standard UML notation with ovals for use cases and lines for associations.

slides.speakerNotes: Use cases model functional requirements from the user's perspective. Focus on goals, not implementation. Actors are roles (Customer, Admin), not specific people. Use cases capture interactions to achieve goals. Explain include (mandatory sub-behavior) vs. extend (optional variation). The diagram provides a high-level view; detailed descriptions come next. ATM example: Withdraw Cash includes Authenticate User.

slides.title: Use Case Descriptions

blocks.content: Structured Template for Detailed Use Case Documentation

content.code:
Use Case: Process Online Order
Actors: Customer, Payment System, Inventory System
Preconditions: Customer is authenticated, cart is not empty
Postconditions: Order is confirmed, inventory updated, payment processed

Main Flow:
1. Customer reviews cart and selects checkout
2. System displays shipping options
3. Customer selects shipping method and enters address
4. System calculates total with shipping and tax
5. Customer enters payment information
6. System validates payment with Payment System
7. System confirms order and sends confirmation email

Alternative Flow 3a: Invalid address
3a.1 System displays address validation error
3a.2 Customer corrects address
3a.3 Resume at step 4

slides.speakerNotes: Detailed use case descriptions complement diagrams. Walk through the template structure: preconditions (what must be true before), postconditions (what's true after), main flow (happy path), alternative flows (exceptions and variations). Emphasize numbering for traceability. Alternative flows handle errors and variations - they're critical for complete requirements. Example 3a shows how to handle invalid input and resume the main flow.

slides.title: User Stories in Agile

blocks.content: As a [role], I want [feature] so that [benefit]

items: INVEST: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable
Acceptance criteria define completion conditions
Lightweight, conversation-focused requirements

content.code:
User Story:
"As a registered user, I want to save items to a wishlist 
so that I can purchase them later"

Acceptance Criteria:
- User can add items from product page to wishlist
- User can view all wishlist items on dedicated page
- User can remove items from wishlist
- Wishlist persists across login sessions
- User receives notification if wishlist item goes on sale

slides.speakerNotes: User stories are the agile alternative to detailed use cases. Format emphasizes role, feature, and business value. INVEST criteria ensure stories are well-formed: Independent (can be developed separately), Negotiable (details can be discussed), Valuable (delivers user value), Estimable (team can estimate effort), Small (fits in sprint), Testable (clear completion criteria). Acceptance criteria are critical - they define 'done'. Compare to use cases: stories are placeholders for conversation, use cases are complete specifications.

slides.title: Requirements Validation

blocks.content: Ensuring Requirements Quality Before Implementation

items: Reviews and Inspections: Peer review, walkthroughs, formal inspections
Prototyping Validation: Stakeholder feedback on mockups
Model Validation: Checking completeness and consistency
Test Case Generation: Deriving tests to verify testability

blocks.content: Validation Checklist: Completeness, Consistency, Feasibility, Testability, Clarity

slides.speakerNotes: Validation ensures requirements are correct before committing to design and implementation. Reviews catch defects early when they're cheapest to fix. Formal inspections use checklists and defined roles (author, moderator, reviewers). Prototypes validate UI and interaction requirements with actual users. Model validation checks for missing scenarios or contradictions. Test case generation verifies each requirement is testable. Emphasize: validation is not the same as verification (which happens after implementation).

slides.title: Requirements Traceability and Management

items: Traceability: Link requirements to sources, design, code, tests
Change Management: Process for requesting and approving changes
Version Control: Track requirements evolution
Impact Analysis: Understand effects of changes

content.prompt: Requirements traceability matrix showing bidirectional arrows connecting: Stakeholder Needs → Requirements → Design Components → Code Modules → Test Cases. Display as a flow diagram with forward traceability arrows going left-to-right and backward traceability arrows going right-to-left. Use different colors for forward and backward traceability.

slides.speakerNotes: Traceability maintains relationships between requirements and other artifacts. Forward traceability: stakeholder need → requirement → design → code → test. Backward traceability: test → code → design → requirement → need. Critical for impact analysis: 'If we change this requirement, what design, code, and tests are affected?' Change management process prevents scope creep: request → evaluate impact → approve/reject → implement → verify. Tools like JIRA, Azure DevOps help manage traceability at scale.

slides.title: Requirements Prioritization

items: MoSCoW: Must have, Should have, Could have, Won't have
Value vs. Effort Matrix: Identify quick wins
Kano Model: Basic, performance, excitement features
Balance business value, risk, and dependencies

content.prompt: 2x2 matrix with axes labeled 'Business Value' (vertical, Low to High) and 'Implementation Effort' (horizontal, Low to High). Four quadrants labeled: High Value/Low Effort = 'Quick Wins', High Value/High Effort = 'Strategic', Low Value/Low Effort = 'Fill-ins', Low Value/High Effort = 'Avoid'. Plot 6-8 sample requirements as dots in different quadrants.

slides.speakerNotes: Prioritization is essential for release planning and managing scope. MoSCoW helps identify MVP (Must-haves only). Value-Effort matrix identifies quick wins (high value, low effort) and items to avoid (low value, high effort). Kano model distinguishes basic features (expected), performance features (more is better), and excitement features (delighters). Stakeholder negotiation is often needed when priorities conflict. Example: Marketing wants feature X for competitive advantage, but Engineering recommends addressing technical debt first.

slides.title: Best Practices and Common Pitfalls

blocks.content: Best Practices

items: Involve stakeholders early and continuously
Use multiple elicitation techniques for triangulation
Validate requirements before implementation
Maintain traceability for impact analysis

blocks.content: Common Pitfalls

items: Gold plating: Unnecessary features → Strict prioritization
Scope creep: Uncontrolled additions → Change control
Ambiguous requirements: Unclear specs → Structured templates
Insufficient validation: Assumed correctness → Systematic reviews

slides.speakerNotes: Synthesize key lessons. Best practices: stakeholder involvement prevents misunderstandings, multiple techniques catch more requirements, early validation prevents costly rework, traceability supports change management. Common pitfalls with mitigations: gold plating (building unnecessary features) - use strict prioritization; scope creep (uncontrolled additions) - enforce change control; ambiguity (unclear specs) - use templates and reviews; insufficient validation (assuming correctness) - implement systematic validation. Share success story: agile project reduced rework 40% through incremental requirements refinement.

slides.title: Summary and Next Steps

blocks.content: Key Takeaways

items: Requirements engineering is systematic: elicitation, analysis, specification, validation, management
Multiple elicitation techniques reveal different requirement types
Distinguish functional (what) from non-functional (how well) requirements
Document using use cases, user stories, and structured specifications
Validate early, manage changes, maintain traceability

blocks.content: Next: Apply these concepts in your project - create SRS document with requirements, use cases, and traceability matrix

slides.speakerNotes: Conclude by reinforcing the five key learning objectives. Requirements engineering is the foundation for successful software projects - getting requirements right prevents costly rework later. Emphasize the connection to upcoming lectures: requirements inform architecture decisions (Lecture 9) and drive testing strategies (Lecture 12). Preview the assignment: students will create a complete SRS document for a medium-sized system, applying all techniques learned today. Encourage questions and provide office hours for assignment support.

The activity requires applying process knowledge to a realistic scenario, exceeding the understand-level objective.

objectiveAlignments.objective: Apply various requirements elicitation techniques to gather stakeholder needs effectively
objectiveAlignments.rationale: Slides 4-6 systematically address this objective at the apply level. Slide 4 requires selecting appropriate techniques for three different scenarios with justification. Slide 5 has students design interview questions for a library system. Slide 6 requires choosing between observation and prototyping for medical and consumer contexts. All activities involve applying elicitation techniques to realistic situations.

objectiveAlignments.objective: Distinguish between functional and non-functional requirements and categorize them appropriately
objectiveAlignments.rationale: Slides 7-9 address this at the analyze level. Slide 2's activity includes basic categorization (A-E statements). Slide 8's activity requires classifying requirements AND identifying quality issues, which involves breaking down requirements to assess their nature. Slide 9's activity explicitly requires categorizing requirements and recognizing when they span multiple categories (e.g., domain requirements that are also constraints), demonstrating analytical thinking.

objectiveAlignments.rationale: Slides 10-14 cover documentation techniques but remain primarily at the understand level. Slide 7 has students write functional requirements (apply level), but use case slides (12-13) and user stories (14) present templates and examples without requiring students to create complete use cases or stories. Students see what good documentation looks like but don't practice producing it themselves. Missing: activities where students write complete use case descriptions or user stories for given scenarios.

objectiveAlignments.objective: Validate requirements for completeness, consistency, and feasibility
objectiveAlignments.rationale: Slide 8's activity addresses validation at the evaluate level by requiring students to identify quality issues in requirements and assess them against measurability criteria. Students must critique REQ-A and REQ-D as unmeasurable and rewrite them with quantified criteria. Slide 15 presents validation techniques (understand level), but slide 8's activity operationalizes the evaluate-level objective by having students assess requirement quality against established criteria.

objectiveAlignments.objective: Manage requirements changes throughout the software development process
objectiveAlignments.rationale: Slides 16-17 cover requirements management (traceability, change control, prioritization) but remain at the understand level. Slide 3's activity briefly mentions 'What if scope changes mid-development?' but doesn't require students to work through change management processes. Missing: activities where students perform impact analysis, evaluate change requests, or apply prioritization frameworks to make trade-off decisions. Content is presented but not practiced.

gaps: Create-level activities are completely absent. Students never design complete requirements artifacts from scratch (e.g., create a full SRS section, design a complete use case model for a system, or synthesize requirements from multiple conflicting stakeholder perspectives).

Documentation objective (use cases, scenarios) lacks apply-level practice. Slides 12-14 present templates and examples but don't require students to produce documentation artifacts. Students see what good use cases look like but don't write them.

Requirements management objective lacks application activities. Slides 16-17 explain traceability and change control but don't have students perform impact analysis, evaluate change requests, or work through prioritization trade-offs.

Validation activities are limited to one slide (slide 8). While that activity effectively addresses evaluate-level thinking, additional validation practice across different requirement types would strengthen this critical objective.

No synthesis activities that integrate multiple RE concepts. Students practice individual skills (elicitation technique selection, requirement writing, categorization) but never combine them in realistic end-to-end scenarios like 'elicit, document, and validate requirements for this stakeholder interview transcript.'
suggestions: Add create-level capstone activity: Provide students with a brief system description and stakeholder interview transcripts. Have them produce a mini-SRS section including 5 functional requirements, 3 NFRs, one complete use case description, and a traceability matrix linking requirements to stakeholder needs. This integrates elicitation, documentation, and management objectives at the create level.

Elevate slide 13 (Use Case Descriptions) to apply level: Replace or supplement the example with an activity where students write a complete use case description for a given scenario (e.g., 'Write the use case for a student withdrawing from a course, including preconditions, main flow, and at least two alternative flows').

Add apply-level activity to slide 16 (Requirements Management): Present a change request scenario (e.g., 'Stakeholder requests adding biometric authentication to the login system'). Have students perform impact analysis using a provided traceability matrix, identify affected design/code/test artifacts, and recommend approve/reject with justification.

Strengthen slide 17 (Prioritization) with application: Provide 8-10 requirements with business value and effort estimates. Have students apply MoSCoW categorization and plot them on the Value-Effort matrix, then justify which requirements belong in MVP vs. future releases.

Add evaluate-level activity to slide 15 (Validation): Provide a set of 6-8 requirements with various quality issues (ambiguity, untestability, inconsistency). Have students systematically validate them using the completeness/consistency/feasibility/testability/clarity checklist, identify specific defects, and propose corrections.

Consider adding a create-level activity where students design an elicitation plan: Given a project description (e.g., healthcare appointment scheduling system), have students select 3-4 elicitation techniques, justify their choices, design specific questions/observation protocols, and explain how techniques complement each other for triangulation.

Slide 14 (User Stories) could include apply-level practice: Provide 3-4 feature descriptions and have students write properly formatted user stories with INVEST-compliant acceptance criteria. This would align the documentation objective with its apply-level expectation.

slides.title: Requirements Engineering Fundamentals

blocks.content: Lecture 8: Requirements Engineering Fundamentals

**Today's Challenge**: You'll design a requirements engineering approach for a real system

**By End of Lecture**: Create complete requirements artifacts integrating elicitation, documentation, and validation

content.title: Preview: Diagnose the Requirements Failure
content.instruction: Read this project failure summary. Identify which RE process stage(s) failed and what specific practices could have prevented the failure.
items: **Case**: University registration system launched with 'fast performance' requirement. System handled 50 users acceptably but crashed with 5,000 during actual registration. Developers claimed they met the requirement; stakeholders were furious.
**Your Task**: (1) Which RE stage failed? (2) What specific requirement quality was violated? (3) Write one corrected requirement that would have prevented this failure.
content.explanation: Elicitation and specification stages failed. The requirement violated testability and measurability—'fast' is ambiguous. Corrected: 'System must process course registration requests for 5,000 concurrent users with 95th percentile response time ≤2 seconds.' This previews why systematic RE practices matter.

slides.speakerNotes: Open with the activity to immediately engage students at analyze level and establish real stakes for RE. After discussion, reveal that this reflects actual failures costing millions. Emphasize that today they'll learn and apply systematic practices to prevent such disasters. Preview the capstone: by lecture end, they'll create requirements artifacts for a system scenario, integrating all RE stages. This sets expectations for create-level work and frames the lecture as building toward practical synthesis, not just concept coverage.

slides.title: What is Requirements Engineering?

blocks.content:
**Requirements Engineering**: Systematic process of defining, documenting, and maintaining software requirements

**Key Impact**: 60-70% of software failures trace to requirements issues

**Core Challenge**: Bridge between stakeholder needs and system implementation

content.title: Analyze: Problem vs. Solution Statements
content.instruction: Classify each statement as a valid requirement (problem-focused) or premature solution. Justify your reasoning.
items: A. The system must process 10,000 transactions per second
B. The system must use Apache Kafka for messaging
C. Users must receive order confirmation within 2 seconds
D. The application must be built with React framework
E. The system must support users in 15 languages
content.explanation: Valid requirements: A (performance NFR), C (performance NFR), E (functional). B and D are implementation solutions, not requirements—they constrain how to build, not what to build. Requirements specify the problem; design specifies the solution.

slides.speakerNotes: After presenting the definition, engage students in analytical thinking about what constitutes a proper requirement. Walk through the activity, emphasizing that requirements describe the problem space (what/why) while design addresses solution space (how). Discuss how B and D might be valid if they're genuine constraints from stakeholders, but typically they're premature design decisions. Connect to real failures: Denver Airport baggage system failed partly because requirements mixed business needs with technical solutions. This distinction is foundational for all subsequent RE activities.

slides.title: The Requirements Engineering Process

content.prompt: Circular process diagram showing four connected activities: Elicitation → Analysis → Specification → Validation, with Requirements Management in the center. Include feedback arrows connecting all activities in both directions. Use professional colors and clear labels.

content.title: Apply: Trace Through the RE Process
content.instruction: A stakeholder requests: 'Users complain checkout takes too long.' Trace this through the RE process—what happens at each stage?
items: Elicitation: What questions would you ask? What techniques?
Analysis: What underlying needs might this reveal?
Specification: Draft one concrete requirement
Validation: How would you verify it's correct?
Management: What if scope changes mid-development?
content.explanation: Sample responses: Elicitation—interview users, observe checkout sessions, ask 'How long is acceptable?' Analysis—need for performance improvement, possibly usability issues. Specification—'Checkout process shall complete in ≤30 seconds for 95% of transactions.' Validation—prototype testing, stakeholder review. Management—trace impact to UI design, backend APIs, test cases.

slides.speakerNotes: Present the process model, then engage students in applying it to a realistic scenario. Walk through each stage, emphasizing the iterative nature—validation might reveal the real problem is confusing UI, not speed, requiring new elicitation. Highlight how one vague complaint transforms through systematic RE into testable requirements. Discuss how different elicitation techniques (observation vs interviews) might yield different insights. Connect to next slide's deep dive into elicitation techniques, noting students will soon learn which techniques work best for different situations.

slides.title: Requirements Elicitation Techniques

items: Interviews: Structured and unstructured conversations
Workshops: Facilitated group sessions for collaboration
Observation: Watching users in natural work environment
Prototyping: Using mockups to elicit feedback
Document Analysis: Reviewing existing systems and regulations

content.title: Apply: Select Elicitation Techniques
content.instruction: For each scenario, choose 2-3 techniques and justify your selection:
items: Medical device software—users are surgeons, strict regulations exist
Consumer mobile app—target users are teenagers, no legacy system
Internal HR system replacement—existing workflows documented, users resistant to change
content.explanation: Sample: Medical device—Document analysis (regulations), observation (OR procedures), structured interviews (safety protocols). Mobile app—Prototyping (visual feedback), workshops (collaborative design), unstructured interviews (exploratory needs). HR system—Document analysis (current workflows), observation (actual vs documented processes), workshops (address resistance). Justifications should reference stakeholder characteristics, domain constraints, and technique strengths.

slides.speakerNotes: Present the five core techniques briefly, then immediately engage students in applying them to realistic contexts. The activity requires analytical thinking—students must consider stakeholder characteristics, domain constraints, and technique strengths/limitations. Emphasize that technique selection is not arbitrary; it depends on project context. Discuss how medical device needs documentation for compliance while teenagers respond better to visual prototypes. This bridges to the next slide's deep dive into interviews and workshops, where students will see how to execute these techniques effectively.

slides.title: Interviews and Workshops

items: Structured: Predefined questions, consistent format
Unstructured: Exploratory, open-ended discussions
Workshops: Facilitated group sessions (JAD, brainstorming)
Open-ended questions uncover unstated needs

content.title: Apply: Design Interview Questions
content.instruction: For this scenario, write 3 interview questions (1 structured, 2 open-ended): You're building a library management system. Your stakeholder is a head librarian who manages circulation, cataloging, and patron services.
items: What makes a good vs. poor question?
How do open-ended questions reveal hidden requirements?
content.explanation: Good structured: 'How many books does your library circulate daily?' (quantifiable). Good open-ended: 'Walk me through what happens when a patron reports a lost book' (reveals workflow); 'What frustrates you most about the current system?' (uncovers pain points). Poor: leading questions, yes/no questions, jargon-heavy phrasing. Open-ended questions let stakeholders describe context, workarounds, and priorities in their own terms.

slides.speakerNotes: After presenting techniques, have students apply them by crafting actual interview questions for a realistic scenario. This moves from understanding what interviews are to applying question design principles. Discuss student responses: structured questions gather facts (circulation volume, staff count), while open-ended questions reveal processes and pain points. Emphasize avoiding leading questions ('Don't you think automated renewals would help?') and closed yes/no questions. For workshops, briefly mention JAD sessions and facilitation techniques like dot voting for prioritization. This prepares students for the observation and prototyping techniques on the next slide.

slides.title: Observation and Prototyping

items: Observation: Watch users in natural environment to uncover tacit knowledge
Contextual inquiry: observation + concurrent interviews
Prototyping: Paper → Wireframes → Interactive mockups
Throwaway vs. evolutionary prototypes

content.title: Apply: Choose Your Technique
content.instruction:
For each scenario, select observation OR prototyping and justify your choice:

A) Hospital emergency room triage system—nurses handle critical decisions under time pressure

B) Consumer mobile app for meal planning—target users are busy parents, feature set uncertain
items: What factors make one technique more suitable?
Could you combine both? How?
content.explanation: A) Observation preferred—triage involves tacit expertise, high-stakes workflows, and context-dependent decisions that nurses may not articulate in interviews. Watching actual triage reveals workarounds and decision patterns. B) Prototyping preferred—uncertain requirements benefit from early feedback; low-fidelity mockups quickly validate feature priorities with parents. Combining both: observe current meal-planning behavior, then prototype solutions based on observed pain points.

slides.speakerNotes: This activity elevates the slide from understand to apply by requiring technique selection and justification for realistic contexts. Guide students to consider: observation excels when processes are tacit, complex, or context-dependent (medical workflows, expert tasks); prototyping works when requirements are uncertain or users struggle to articulate needs abstractly. Discuss how observation reveals what people actually do versus what they say, while prototypes make abstract requirements concrete. Emphasize that techniques often combine—observe first to understand context, then prototype solutions. This bridges to functional requirements on the next slide, where documented behaviors come from elicitation.

slides.title: Functional Requirements

blocks.content:
What the system must do - specific behaviors and functions

• Describe system inputs, outputs, and transformations
• Expressed as 'The system shall...' statements
• Directly testable through functional testing

content.title: Apply: Write Functional Requirements
content.instruction:
A university needs a course registration system. Given these stakeholder needs, write 3 functional requirements using proper format:

• Students want to see which courses fit their schedule
• Professors need to know enrollment numbers
• System must prevent double-booking classrooms
items: Use 'The system shall...' format
Make each requirement atomic and testable
Identify inputs, outputs, or transformations
content.explanation: Sample answers: FR-001: The system shall display a visual schedule showing time conflicts when a student selects a course. FR-002: The system shall provide real-time enrollment counts to instructors for their assigned courses. FR-003: The system shall reject room assignments that create scheduling conflicts for the same location and time slot. Each requirement specifies observable system behavior that can be verified through testing.

slides.speakerNotes: This activity elevates the slide from understand to apply by requiring students to transform stakeholder needs into properly formatted functional requirements. After individual work, share sample answers and discuss common mistakes: vague verbs, multiple requirements in one statement, or non-testable phrasing. Emphasize that good FRs specify observable behavior without prescribing implementation. Ask students to identify the input/output/transformation in each requirement. This directly supports the objective to document requirements using industry standards and bridges to NFRs on the next slide, where quality attributes complement functional behavior.

slides.title: Non-Functional Requirements

blocks.content:
How well the system performs - quality attributes that constrain solutions

• Performance, Security, Usability, Reliability, Maintainability
• Drive architectural decisions (NFRs often determine system structure)
• Must be quantified with measurable criteria
• Categories from ISO 25010 quality model

content.title: Analyze: Categorize & Evaluate Requirements
content.instruction: Examine these requirements. For each: (1) Classify as Functional, Non-Functional, or Constraint, (2) Identify quality issues, (3) Rewrite poorly specified NFRs with measurable criteria.
items: REQ-A: System must be very fast and responsive
REQ-B: System shall generate monthly reports in PDF format
REQ-C: Application must be developed using React framework
REQ-D: System should be easy to use for all users
content.explanation: REQ-A: NFR (performance) - too vague. Better: 'System shall load pages within 1.5 seconds for 95% of requests.' REQ-B: Functional - specifies system behavior. REQ-C: Constraint - mandates technology choice. REQ-D: NFR (usability) - unmeasurable. Better: 'Users shall complete core tasks with ≤3 clicks and no training.' This exercise develops analyze-level skills for distinguishing requirement types and evaluate-level skills for assessing quality against measurability criteria.

slides.speakerNotes: This activity addresses two objectives: distinguishing functional/non-functional requirements (analyze level) and validating requirement quality (evaluate level). After individual work, discuss classifications and common NFR mistakes: vague terms without metrics. Emphasize that NFRs like 'fast' or 'user-friendly' are untestable. Show how quantified NFRs drive architecture: 99.9% availability requires redundancy; sub-second response times may necessitate caching layers. Connect to validation criteria on slide 15 and architectural impact discussions.

slides.title: Constraints and Domain Requirements

blocks.content:
Constraints: Non-negotiable limitations (technology mandates, regulations, budget)
Domain Requirements: Application-specific needs from the problem domain (medical, financial, legal)

Both limit solution space and drive architectural decisions

content.title: Analyze: Classify Requirements
content.instruction: Categorize each requirement as Functional, Non-Functional, Constraint, or Domain Requirement. Justify your classification and identify any that span multiple categories.
items: System must use PostgreSQL 12 or higher
Healthcare records must be retained for 7 years
Users shall reset passwords via email verification
Payment processing must comply with PCI-DSS Level 1
System shall process 10,000 transactions per second
Application must be deployed on AWS infrastructure
content.explanation: PostgreSQL requirement: Constraint (technology mandate). 7-year retention: Domain requirement AND constraint (legal/healthcare domain). Password reset: Functional (system behavior). PCI-DSS: Domain requirement AND constraint (payment domain + regulation). 10K TPS: Non-functional (performance). AWS deployment: Constraint (platform mandate). Some requirements span categories—recognizing overlaps requires analytical thinking about requirement nature and origin.

slides.speakerNotes: This activity addresses the analyze-level objective for distinguishing requirement types. After individual classification, discuss borderline cases that span categories—many domain requirements also function as constraints. Emphasize that constraints narrow design choices (PostgreSQL eliminates NoSQL options), while domain requirements reflect specialized knowledge (HIPAA, PCI-DSS require domain expertise to identify). Connect to slide 8's NFR discussion and slide 10's documentation structure. Ask: How would you discover domain requirements during elicitation? What happens if domain constraints are missed early?

slides.title: Requirements Specification Documents

blocks.content:
IEEE 830 / ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 Standard Structure:

1. Introduction: Purpose, scope, definitions, overview
2. Overall Description: Product perspective, functions, user characteristics
3. Specific Requirements: Detailed functional and non-functional requirements
4. Appendices: Models, analysis, supporting information

Quality Characteristics: Clear, Unambiguous, Testable, Consistent, Complete

content.title: Apply: Structure an SRS Section
content.instruction:
You're documenting requirements for a university course registration system. Using the IEEE 830 structure, organize these items into the correct SRS sections (Introduction, Overall Description, Specific Requirements, or Appendices). Then identify which quality characteristic each violates:

• 'Students can register for courses'
• Glossary defining 'prerequisite', 'credit hour', 'waitlist'
• 'System should be user-friendly'
• Entity-relationship diagram of course-student relationships
• Target users: undergraduate/graduate students, faculty advisors
• 'The system shall allow students to add courses to their schedule if prerequisites are met and seats are available'
content.explanation: Correct placement: Glossary→Introduction; User types→Overall Description; ER diagram→Appendices; Three requirements→Specific Requirements. Quality issues: 'can register' is ambiguous (missing constraints), 'user-friendly' is untestable (no criteria), last requirement is clear and testable. This apply-level activity supports the documentation objective by having students practice organizing content into standard SRS structure while evaluating requirement quality.

slides.speakerNotes: This activity elevates the slide from understand to apply level by requiring students to actively use the IEEE 830 structure rather than just reading about it. After individual work, discuss why proper organization matters: stakeholders find information predictably, reviewers can verify completeness section-by-section, and developers know where to look for specific requirement types. Highlight that the poorly-written requirements would go in Specific Requirements but need improvement first—this bridges to slide 11's quality guidelines. Ask: What happens if requirements are scattered randomly through a document? How does standard structure support validation?

slides.title: Writing Quality Requirements

items: Modal verbs: 'shall' (mandatory), 'should' (desirable), 'may' (optional)
Avoid ambiguous terms without quantification
One requirement per statement (atomic)
Each requirement must be verifiable

content.code:
❌ Poor: 'The system should be secure and easy to use'

✓ Good: 'The system shall require authentication using 
   username and password before accessing user data'

❌ Poor: 'The system will handle lots of users'

✓ Good: 'The system shall support 10,000 concurrent 
   users with response time < 3 seconds'

content.title: Requirement Quality Analysis
content.instructions:
Evaluate these requirements using the quality checklist (clear, unambiguous, testable, consistent, atomic). Identify specific defects in each:

1. 'The mobile app shall be fast and responsive'
2. 'The system must support many payment methods and be secure'
3. 'Users should be able to easily search for products'

For each defect found, rewrite the requirement to fix it. Be specific and quantifiable.
content.deliverable: List of defects identified and corrected requirements

slides.speakerNotes: After reviewing the guidelines and examples, students now apply quality criteria to evaluate and correct poorly-written requirements. Walk through the activity: requirement 1 lacks quantification (how fast?), 2 violates atomicity (two requirements), 3 is ambiguous (easily?). Students should produce corrected versions like 'The mobile app shall load the home screen within 2 seconds on 4G networks.' This apply-level activity directly supports the documentation objective and prepares students for writing complete use cases in upcoming slides.

slides.title: Use Case Fundamentals

blocks.content: Description of system behavior from user perspective to achieve a goal

items: Actors: Users or external systems
Use Cases: Goals the actors want to achieve
Relationships: Include, extend, generalization

content.prompt: UML use case diagram for online shopping system. Show Customer actor (stick figure) connected to use cases: Browse Products, Add to Cart, Checkout, Track Order. Show Admin actor connected to Manage Inventory. Include 'Authenticate User' use case with <<include>> relationship to Checkout. Use standard UML notation with ovals for use cases and lines for associations.

slides.speakerNotes: Use cases model functional requirements from the user's perspective. Focus on goals, not implementation. Actors are roles (Customer, Admin), not specific people. Use cases capture interactions to achieve goals. Explain include (mandatory sub-behavior) vs. extend (optional variation). The diagram provides a high-level view; detailed descriptions come next. ATM example: Withdraw Cash includes Authenticate User.

slides.title: Use Case Descriptions

blocks.content: Structured Template for Detailed Use Case Documentation

content.code:
Use Case: [Name]
Actors: [Primary and secondary actors]
Preconditions: [What must be true before execution]
Postconditions: [System state after successful completion]

Main Flow:
1. [Actor action]
2. [System response]
...

Alternative Flow [step]a: [Exception/variation name]
[step]a.1 [How system handles the exception]
[step]a.2 [Resume point or termination]

content.title: Write a Complete Use Case
content.instructions: Scenario: A university student wants to drop a course before the deadline. Write a complete use case description including: actors, preconditions, postconditions, main flow (at least 5 steps), and two alternative flows (e.g., past deadline, course required for major). Use the template structure provided above.
content.deliverable: Complete use case description following the template format

slides.speakerNotes: This activity elevates use case knowledge to apply level by requiring students to create documentation from scratch. Provide the template, then have students work individually. Emphasize: preconditions establish context, postconditions define success state, main flow is the happy path, alternative flows handle exceptions. Common student mistakes: forgetting to resume main flow, writing implementation details instead of user-system interactions, incomplete preconditions. After 8 minutes, share 1-2 student examples and discuss completeness. This directly addresses the documentation objective's apply-level expectation.

slides.title: User Stories in Agile

blocks.content: As a [role], I want [feature] so that [benefit]

items: INVEST: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable
Acceptance criteria define 'done' and enable testing
Lightweight alternative to detailed use cases

content.title: Write User Stories with Acceptance Criteria
content.instructions: You're building a library management system. Write properly formatted user stories with complete acceptance criteria for these features: (1) Student reserves a book online, (2) Librarian processes overdue fines, (3) Faculty member requests book purchase. Each story must follow the role-feature-benefit format and include 3-5 testable acceptance criteria. Ensure stories meet INVEST criteria.
content.deliverable: Three complete user stories with acceptance criteria

slides.speakerNotes: This activity elevates the slide to apply level, directly addressing the documentation objective gap. Students must create user stories from feature descriptions, not just read examples. Emphasize the role-feature-benefit structure captures business value, while acceptance criteria make stories testable. Common mistakes: vague acceptance criteria, missing the 'so that' benefit clause, stories too large or dependent. After 7 minutes, share one student example per feature and evaluate against INVEST criteria as a class. This practice bridges agile documentation techniques with the broader requirements documentation objective.

slides.title: Requirements Validation

blocks.content: Ensuring Requirements Quality Before Implementation

items: Reviews: Peer review, walkthroughs, formal inspections with checklists
Prototyping: Validate UI/interaction requirements with stakeholders
Model Validation: Check completeness, consistency, missing scenarios
Quality Criteria: Completeness, Consistency, Feasibility, Testability, Clarity

content.title: Validate Requirements and Identify Defects
content.instructions: Review these six requirements for an online course registration system using the validation checklist (completeness, consistency, feasibility, testability, clarity): (1) 'The system shall be user-friendly', (2) 'Students can register for courses', (3) 'System responds quickly to user actions', (4) 'Students must complete prerequisites before registering for advanced courses', (5) 'Maximum class size is 30 students and unlimited for online courses', (6) 'Registration confirmation sent via email within 24 hours'. Identify specific quality defects in each requirement and propose corrected versions.
content.deliverable: Defect analysis with corrections for all six requirements

slides.speakerNotes: This evaluate-level activity addresses the validation objective gap by requiring students to systematically apply quality criteria to actual requirements. Requirements contain deliberate defects: vague terms (user-friendly, quickly), missing preconditions, inconsistencies, and untestable criteria. After 8 minutes, discuss findings. Requirement 1 lacks measurable criteria; 2 is incomplete (missing constraints); 3 is untestable; 4 needs explicit prerequisite checking mechanism; 5 has contradictory constraints; 6 is testable but may be infeasible. Emphasize validation catches defects before costly implementation. This practice strengthens critical requirements quality assessment skills.

slides.title: Requirements Traceability and Management

items: Traceability: Link requirements to sources, design, code, tests
Change Management: Process for requesting and approving changes
Impact Analysis: Understand ripple effects of changes
Version Control: Track requirements evolution over time

content.prompt: Requirements traceability matrix showing bidirectional arrows connecting: Stakeholder Needs → Requirements → Design Components → Code Modules → Test Cases. Display as a flow diagram with forward traceability arrows going left-to-right and backward traceability arrows going right-to-left. Use different colors for forward and backward traceability.

content.title: Perform Impact Analysis for Change Request
content.instructions: A stakeholder requests adding biometric fingerprint authentication to replace password login (Req-12). Using the provided traceability matrix showing Req-12 traces to: LoginUI design component, AuthenticationModule code, and 8 test cases (TC-45 through TC-52). Perform impact analysis: (1) List all artifacts affected by this change, (2) Identify new artifacts needed, (3) Estimate effort as Low/Medium/High, (4) Recommend approve/reject with justification considering security benefits vs. implementation cost.
content.deliverable: Impact analysis report with approval recommendation

slides.speakerNotes: This apply-level activity addresses the requirements management objective gap by having students work through a realistic change request scenario. Students must trace dependencies using the provided matrix, identify cascading impacts across design/code/test layers, and make a justified decision. After 7 minutes, discuss findings. Expected impacts: LoginUI redesign, AuthenticationModule rewrite, hardware integration, all 8 tests must be updated, plus new biometric tests needed. High effort but high security value. Emphasize that traceability enables systematic impact analysis, preventing overlooked dependencies. This practice develops critical change management skills needed in real projects.

slides.title: Requirements Prioritization

items: MoSCoW: Must have, Should have, Could have, Won't have
Value vs. Effort Matrix: Identify quick wins and items to avoid
Kano Model: Basic, performance, excitement features
Balance business value, technical risk, and dependencies

content.prompt: 2x2 matrix with axes labeled 'Business Value' (vertical, Low to High) and 'Implementation Effort' (horizontal, Low to High). Four quadrants labeled: High Value/Low Effort = 'Quick Wins', High Value/High Effort = 'Strategic', Low Value/Low Effort = 'Fill-ins', Low Value/High Effort = 'Avoid'. Show empty matrix ready for plotting requirements.

content.title: Apply Prioritization Frameworks
content.instructions: You have 10 requirements for an e-commerce system with business value (1-10) and effort estimates (1-10 story points): R1-Checkout(V:9,E:3), R2-Wishlist(V:4,E:2), R3-Reviews(V:7,E:5), R4-PaymentGateway(V:10,E:8), R5-SearchFilters(V:8,E:4), R6-SocialShare(V:3,E:6), R7-OrderTracking(V:9,E:7), R8-GuestCheckout(V:6,E:2), R9-Recommendations(V:5,E:9), R10-MultiCurrency(V:7,E:8). Tasks: (1) Categorize each using MoSCoW for MVP release, (2) Plot all on Value-Effort matrix, (3) Identify top 3 MVP requirements with justification.
content.deliverable: MoSCoW categories, plotted matrix, justified MVP selection

slides.speakerNotes: This apply-level activity addresses the requirements management objective gap by having students work through realistic prioritization trade-offs. Students must apply multiple frameworks (MoSCoW, Value-Effort matrix) to make defensible decisions about MVP scope. After 8 minutes, discuss results. Expected MVP: R1, R4, R5 (high value, manageable effort). R4 is Must despite high effort (payment essential). R6 and R9 should be Won't/Avoid (low value, high effort). Emphasize that prioritization requires balancing stakeholder desires against constraints. This develops critical release planning skills needed when resources are limited.

slides.title: Best Practices and Common Pitfalls

blocks.content: Best Practices

items: Involve stakeholders early and continuously
Use multiple elicitation techniques for triangulation
Validate requirements before implementation
Maintain traceability for impact analysis

blocks.content: Common Pitfalls

items: Gold plating: Unnecessary features → Strict prioritization
Scope creep: Uncontrolled additions → Change control
Ambiguous requirements: Unclear specs → Structured templates
Insufficient validation: Assumed correctness → Systematic reviews

slides.speakerNotes: Synthesize key lessons. Best practices: stakeholder involvement prevents misunderstandings, multiple techniques catch more requirements, early validation prevents costly rework, traceability supports change management. Common pitfalls with mitigations: gold plating (building unnecessary features) - use strict prioritization; scope creep (uncontrolled additions) - enforce change control; ambiguity (unclear specs) - use templates and reviews; insufficient validation (assuming correctness) - implement systematic validation. Share success story: agile project reduced rework 40% through incremental requirements refinement.

slides.title: Summary and Next Steps

blocks.content: Key Takeaways

items: Requirements engineering is systematic: elicitation, analysis, specification, validation, management
Multiple elicitation techniques reveal different requirement types
Distinguish functional (what) from non-functional (how well) requirements
Document using use cases, user stories, and structured specifications
Validate early, manage changes, maintain traceability

blocks.content: Next: Apply these concepts in your project - create SRS document with requirements, use cases, and traceability matrix

slides.speakerNotes: Conclude by reinforcing the five key learning objectives. Requirements engineering is the foundation for successful software projects - getting requirements right prevents costly rework later. Emphasize the connection to upcoming lectures: requirements inform architecture decisions (Lecture 9) and drive testing strategies (Lecture 12). Preview the assignment: students will create a complete SRS document for a medium-sized system, applying all techniques learned today. Encourage questions and provide office hours for assignment support.
